title: Loma Wells: Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Loma wells have a 40 ft median depth, but records range to 547 ft. See yield, water levels, risks and estimated drilling costs.
h1: What Loma, Colorado Well Records Tell a Buyer
intro_html:
Buying land near Loma means looking past the asking price and checking the water record. Within 5 miles of Loma, Colorado, DWR records show 166 permitted wells, although only 58 are recorded as constructed. Of those, 55 report a total depth, 8 report a pump yield and 4 report a static water level.

The local records point to shallow wells in many locations, but they also show a wide spread in depth and limited production data. That makes neighboring well checks, a proper site evaluation and a written drilling estimate important before you buy or build.

sections.heading: Loma well depth depends on the ground below the lot
sections.html:
The median reported well depth near Loma is 40 feet. The middle half runs from 21 to 248 feet, so the median is not a reliable promise for every parcel. The 90th percentile reaches 423 feet, and the deepest record is 547 feet.

Depth records are concentrated in the shallow range: 62% are under 100 feet, 15% are between 100 and 300 feet, and 24% are between 300 and 600 feet. That spread matters when comparing drilling bids. A nearby shallow well may not represent your lot if the sedimentary and alluvial ground changes, or if the driller encounters a less productive layer or fractured bedrock.

Ask for nearby completed-well depths, casing and grout details, and a bid that explains what happens if the target depth does not produce usable water.

sections.heading: Expected well yield around Loma
sections.html:
Only 8 wells in the records report a pump yield, so the yield statistics are useful but not highly complete. Among those reports, the median yield is 4.5 gallons per minute, with the middle half from 3.0 to 11.0 gallons per minute.

Half of the reported wells produce between 1 and 5 gallons per minute, while 38% produce between 5 and 15 gallons per minute and 12% produce more than 15 gallons per minute. No reported well is under 1 gallon per minute.

A 4.5 gallon-per-minute result can serve a household when the well, pressure tank and storage are designed appropriately, but it is not the same as unlimited water. Confirm the well's permitted use, pump test results and recovery before assuming it will support irrigation, livestock or a larger home.

sections.heading: What the Loma water-level records show
sections.html:
Only 4 wells report a static water level, so there is not enough local information to establish a dependable long-term trend. The reported median depth to static water is 45 feet, and the middle half runs from 8 to 86 feet.

Those figures suggest that water may be relatively shallow in some parts of the Loma area, but they do not show that the water table is stable across every property. Static water level also changes with season, pumping and the way the measurement was taken.

The permits identify an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer for 165 wells. No wells are identified in a Denver Basin aquifer. Before closing, obtain the driller's log and ask how the water level was measured. A current test on the actual property is more useful than treating the area median as a guarantee.

sections.heading: Loma permit history and the drillers in the record
sections.html:
Permit activity increased sharply after the early records. The database shows 3 permits in the 1960s, 1 in the 1970s, 4 in the 1980s, 50 in the 1990s, 35 in the 2000s, 38 in the 2010s and 7 in the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2022.

Many permits are for monitoring: monitoring wells make up 52% of the use mix. Domestic or household wells account for 19%, irrigation 6% and stock 4%. That mix is important because the total permit count is not the same as the number of household water supplies.

The most active driller listed is Authorized (Pe, Pg), followed by Rocky Mountain Drlg./Pump Svcs (Wisener, A. L.) and Colorado Drilling Company (Carns, Don R). Use the permit record to identify nearby work, then verify completion details directly with the county and Colorado DWR.

sections.heading: Estimated cost to drill a Loma well
sections.html:
For Loma's mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground, the drilling rate model is $50 to $75 per foot. At the local median depth of 40 feet, the drilled hole is estimated at about $2,000 to $3,000.

That is only the hole. A finished well with pump, pressure tank, trenching and electrical is estimated at $8,000 to $15,000. A deeper-than-median hole, difficult access, additional casing or changing ground conditions can move the final price above that range.

When comparing bids, separate drilling from the pump system and site work. Ask whether the price includes casing, grout, development, a pump test, electrical connection and disposal of cuttings. Also ask for the cost if the first hole is dry or produces less water than the permit requires.

sections.heading: Loma water risks and site checks before construction
sections.html:
The records show 21 PFAS sampling or contamination sites within about 10 miles, along with 1 historic mine feature and 1 EPA Superfund or cleanup site. A mapped site does not prove that a particular well is contaminated, but it is a reason to review environmental records and test the water before relying on it.

Low yield and dry holes remain practical risks because the aquifer is listed as unnamed or fractured bedrock for nearly all recorded wells, and reported yield data are limited. Test for bacteria, nitrates and any site-specific contaminants recommended by a qualified professional.

Before building, confirm well location, septic separation, access for a drill rig, power routing and the permitted use. A household-use well may have limits, and an exempt well in an over-appropriated basin can require an augmentation plan. Check the permit rather than assuming the well can support every planned use.

sections.heading: A sensible buying plan for a Loma lot
sections.html:
Start with the exact parcel, not just the Loma area statistics. Pull nearby permits and completion reports, prioritizing wells in comparable ground and close to the proposed house site. Fruita is about 5 miles away, while Redlands and Grand Junction are about 12 and 15 miles away; those places provide broader context but should not replace parcel-specific evidence.

For an existing home, request the well permit, construction report, pump test, water-quality results and maintenance history. For vacant land, make the purchase contract contingent on a well feasibility review and a clear estimate for drilling, pumping equipment, trenching and electrical work.

Plan the house, septic system and driveway together. Preserve drill-rig access, keep the well away from contamination sources, and have a Colorado water-rights professional confirm the permitted use before counting on irrigation or additional connections.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Loma, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported depth near Loma is 40 feet. The middle half of reported wells ranges from 21 to 248 feet, but the 90th percentile is 423 feet and the deepest record is 547 feet. Most recorded wells are under 100 feet, yet the wide range means nearby well logs are more useful than the median alone.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Loma?
faq.a: The local cost model uses $50 to $75 per foot for mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground. At the 40-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $2,000 to $3,000. A finished system, including pump, tank, trenching and electrical, is estimated at $8,000 to $15,000. Difficult ground or greater depth can increase the total.

faq.q: How much water do Loma wells produce?
faq.a: Only 8 local records report a pump yield. Those reported wells have a median yield of 4.5 gallons per minute, with the middle half from 3.0 to 11.0 gallons per minute. Half report between 1 and 5 gallons per minute. Treat these figures as a guide, not a guarantee for an untested parcel.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Loma, Colorado?
faq.a: Safety depends on the individual well and its location. Records show 21 PFAS sampling or contamination sites within about 10 miles, plus 1 historic mine feature and 1 EPA Superfund or cleanup site. Those mapped sites do not establish contamination at your property. Test the well for routine and location-specific contaminants before drinking it.

faq.q: Are Loma wells running out of water?
faq.a: The available records do not establish a declining water-table trend. Only 4 wells report static water levels, with a median depth to water of 45 feet and a middle half from 8 to 86 feet. Because the dataset is small, request a current static-level measurement, pump test and nearby completion records before buying.
